c.tagline: The world's highest capital, strung between snowcapped peaks by cable car.

taxi.color: white with checkered stripe (radio taxis) / varied for street taxis
taxi.fareNote: Street taxis negotiate a flat fare before the ride (no meters); typically 15-25 Bs for short trips within a zone, more between zones like Centro to Zona Sur. Radio/app taxis (Uber, inDrive) show fares upfront.

emergency.note: Fire brigade 119; tourist police (POLTUR) available in Plaza del Estadio/Sopocachi for reporting incidents to foreigners.

avoid.reason: Fake-police / 'express kidnapping' scams; use official radio taxis; caution in El Alto and at night

hood_desc: Bustling backpacker and cultural core packed with markets (Witches' Market, San Francisco Church), budget hostels, and tour operators; best for first-timers wanting to walk everywhere and dive into local life, though noisy and busy.

Leafy, cosmopolitan district with cafes, nightlife, art-house cinemas, and boutique hotels; suits travelers who want a residential-feel base with good restaurants a short taxi/teleferico ride from the sights.

Quiet, affluent southern district with malls, embassies, and manicured streets at a lower, warmer elevation; suits business travelers, families, and those wanting comfort and easier breathing (lower altitude).

Upscale southern zone with La Paz's best restaurants, art galleries, and international brands; suits travelers wanting a polished, safe, semi-suburban base with easy access to the Zona Sur dining scene.
Quiet, mid-altitude residential neighborhood between the center and Zona Sur, popular with longer-term visitors and volunteers for its calmer streets and easy teleferico access to downtown.

water.note: Avoid tap water; stick to bottled or purified water.

transit.pay: Mi Teleférico uses a rechargeable smart card (or single-journey token) tapped at turnstiles, with flat fares around 3 Bs per line (2 Bs at some interchange stations); PumaKatari buses accept cash or a similar smart card; minibuses and trufis are cash-only, paid to the driver or conductor on board.
transit.hours: Mi Teleférico generally runs about 6am-11pm (some lines to midnight); PumaKatari buses run roughly 6am-10pm; minibuses/trufis run early morning to around 9-10pm with sparse late-night coverage.
transit.note: Mi Teleférico is the signature system - the world's longest and highest urban cable car network, linking hillside El Alto with the La Paz basin and offering spectacular views; it is often faster and more comfortable than road transit due to the city's brutal traffic and steep terrain.

train: Ferrocarril Andino (limited regional freight/passenger service; no major intercity passenger rail hub in La Paz)
bus: Terminal de Buses La Paz (Av. Perú) for intercity coaches to Cochabamba, Oruro, Sucre, Uyuni, Copacabana, and international routes to Peru, Chile, Argentina
ferry: Lake Titicaca ferries/launches from Copacabana (day-trip distance from La Paz)

airport.name: El Alto International Airport (LPB)
airport.drive: 20-40 min depending on traffic (airport sits above city at ~4,061m, city center down in the canyon)

transit.m: Cotranstur airport bus to Sopocachi/Plaza San Francisco (~38 min)

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up or 5-10% at sit-down restaurants is appreciated but not expected. Taxi drivers and market vendors are not typically tipped.

food.name: Saltenas
food.desc: Bolivia's juicy baked pastry filled with beef or chicken, potato, peas, olive and a sweet-spicy gravy; eaten standing up, mid-morning only.

places.name: Pacena La Saltena
places.note: The city's benchmark saltena chain; go before 11am while they are still hot.

places.name: Los Amigos
places.note: Known for flaky saltenas de hojaldre and picante surtido; busy at lunchtime.

places.name: El Hornito
places.note: Neighbourhood bakery-style saltenas with a strong local following.

food.name: Anticuchos
food.desc: Charcoal-grilled beef-heart skewers with a boiled potato and peanut-chilli sauce, sold from smoky street carts after dark.

places.name: Anticuchos Dona Lidia
places.note: The most-named anticucho cart in La Paz; queues form from about 7pm.

places.name: Plaza Avaroa evening carts
places.note: Cluster of grills around the plaza; pick the one with the longest local queue.

places.name: Mercado Lanza
places.area: Casco Viejo, near Plaza San Francisco
places.note: Covered market food floor with cheap grilled skewers and soups all day.

food.name: Silpancho
food.desc: Pounded breaded beef cutlet over rice and sliced potato, topped with a fried egg and chopped tomato-onion salsa - Bolivia's most filling plate.

places.name: El Super Silpancho Orejas de Elefante
places.note: Specialist named for its elephant-ear-sized cutlets; portions are huge.

places.name: Phayawi
places.note: Regional Bolivian menu including a well-regarded silpancho cochabambino.

places.name: Mercado Lanza
places.note: Market comedor stalls serving silpancho and milanesa at local prices.

food.name: Api con pastel
food.desc: Hot purple-corn drink thickened with cinnamon and clove, served with a deep-fried cheese pastry dusted in sugar - the classic Andean breakfast.

places.name: Mercado Lanza
places.note: Upstairs comedor stalls serve api and pastel from dawn; cheapest breakfast in town.

places.name: Mercado Rodriguez
places.note: Sprawling street market with api stands among the produce sellers.

places.name: Mercado Camacho
places.note: Tidy covered market popular with office workers for morning api con pastel.

food.name: Sopa de mani
food.desc: Ground-peanut soup with beef, potato and pasta, finished with crisp shoestring fries and parsley; a staple of Bolivian set lunches.

places.name: Popular Cocina Boliviana
places.note: Small daily-changing Bolivian tasting lunch; book ahead, it fills fast.

places.name: Mercado Lanza
places.note: Market stalls ladle sopa de mani as part of a cheap two-course almuerzo.

places.name: Phayawi
places.note: Regional Bolivian cooking with soups from several departments.

food.name: Fricase paceno
food.desc: La Paz's own pork stew in a yellow aji amarillo broth with hominy corn and chuno freeze-dried potato; traditionally a weekend hangover cure.

places.name: Mercado Rodriguez
places.note: Weekend market stalls serve fricase from early morning, as locals do.

places.name: Mercado Camacho
places.note: Covered market comedores with reliable fricase and chairo soups.

places.name: Popular Cocina Boliviana
places.note: Refined versions of paceno home cooking on a short rotating menu.

food.name: Singani (chuflay)
food.desc: Bolivia's high-altitude muscat grape brandy, drunk neat or as a chuflay with ginger ale and lime; protected as a national spirit.

places.name: Gustu
places.note: Bolivia-only ingredients and an outstanding singani list; the city's landmark restaurant.

places.name: Diesel Nacional
places.note: Industrial-themed bar, long-running Sopocachi nightlife fixture for chuflays.

places.name: Popular Cocina Boliviana
places.note: Serves singani cocktails alongside its Bolivian lunch menu.

food.name: Mocochinchi
food.desc: Chilled sweet infusion of dried peaches with cinnamon and clove, ladled from glass barrels on the street; the local answer to iced tea.

places.name: Calle Sagarnaga street vendors
places.area: Casco Viejo, near Plaza San Francisco
places.note: Glass-barrel carts along the tourist market street; cheap and refreshing.

places.name: Mercado Lanza
places.note: Sold by the glass beside the api and juice stalls.

places.name: Mercado Rodriguez
places.note: Vendors sell mocochinchi and linaza alongside fruit juices.

landmarks: Valle de la Luna (Moon Valley)
A surreal maze of eroded clay spires and canyons on La Paz's outskirts, resembling a lunar landscape carved by centuries of wind and rain.
Mi Teleférico
The world's highest and longest urban cable car network, offering breathtaking aerial views over La Paz's canyon-set cityscape and snowcapped peaks.
Witches' Market (Mercado de las Brujas)
An atmospheric market of dried llama fetuses, herbal remedies, and Andean amulets, revealing La Paz's enduring indigenous mystical traditions.
Basílica de San Francisco
A richly decorated 16th-century church blending Spanish colonial and indigenous Andean stone carving, anchoring La Paz's bustling historic center.
Plaza Murillo
La Paz's grand main square, flanked by the presidential palace and cathedral, alive with pigeons, vendors, and the pulse of Bolivian politics.
Mirador Killi Killi
A hilltop lookout delivering one of the most spectacular panoramic views of La Paz's bowl-shaped valley and the snowcapped Illimani beyond.
Calle Jaén
A beautifully preserved cobblestone colonial street lined with pastel facades and small museums, evoking La Paz's 18th-century charm.
Catedral Metropolitana de La Paz
An imposing neoclassical cathedral overlooking Plaza Murillo, its grand columned facade dominating the city's spiritual and civic heart.
Mount Illimani viewpoint
The snowcapped 6,438-meter sentinel peak that looms over La Paz, its glistening summit forming the city's most iconic and photographed backdrop.
Mercado Lanza
A vibrant central market piled high with fresh produce, juices, and local delicacies, capturing the everyday rhythm of highland Bolivian life.

train.note: There is no passenger train from La Paz itself. The nearest service is Ferroviaria Andina's (FCA) Expreso del Sur and Wara Wara del Sur, which start in Oruro (about 4h by bus from La Paz) and run south to Uyuni, Tupiza and Villazón on the Argentine border, where you cross on foot to La Quiaca. Tickets are sold at Oruro station or through FCA.

bus.note: International coaches leave from the main Terminal de Buses de La Paz; Trans Salvador is the established cross-border operator to southern Peru and northern Chile. Carry your passport for the Desaguadero (Peru) or Tambo Quemado (Chile) crossings and expect a change of bus at some borders.

ferry.note: Bolivia is landlocked, so there are no international ferries. On nearby Lake Titicaca, small local boats and hydrofoils serve Copacabana, Isla del Sol and the Isla del Sol crossings, and a vehicle barge crosses the Strait of Tiquina — all domestic.

full.name: Cochabamba
full.blurb: Bolivian city known for its valley setting, mild climate, and rich culinary tradition.

full.name: Juliaca
full.blurb: High-altitude Andean city near Lake Titicaca known for trade and traditional markets.

full.name: Oruro
full.blurb: High-altitude Bolivian mining city famed for its colorful Carnival celebrations.

full.name: Puno
full.blurb: High-altitude Andean city on Lake Titicaca, known for vibrant folk festivals and traditions.

full.name: Sacaba
full.blurb: Andean valley city in Bolivia known for farming and traditional markets.
